# Follow-Up Intervals and Referral Guidance for Diabetic Retinopathy
Source: American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) Preferred Practice Pattern
(PPP) for Diabetic Retinopathy; ICO/ADA screening guidance. (Paraphrased
summary for internal knowledge-base use -- consult the current official AAO
PPP document for authoritative, up-to-date clinical guidance.)

## Screening initiation
  - Type 1 diabetes: first dilated eye exam ~5 years after diagnosis.
  - Type 2 diabetes: first dilated eye exam at time of diagnosis (retinopathy
    may already be present given typically delayed T2D diagnosis).
  - Pregnant patients with pre-existing diabetes: examine promptly after
    conception; follow every 3-12 months depending on severity, since
    pregnancy can accelerate progression. Gestational diabetes alone does
    not require a dedicated eye exam.

## Recommended follow-up interval by severity (routine, non-pregnant adult)
  - No DR or minimal/mild NPDR, no DME: re-examine in ~12 months
    (some protocols suggest 12-24 months for true no-DR cases).
  - Moderate NPDR: follow-up in an interval shorter than 12 months --
    commonly cited as every 6-9 months, more frequent in populations with
    documented faster progression.
  - Severe NPDR (or worse) or any clinically significant DME: refer to an
    eye care professional / retina specialist for evaluation and likely
    treatment; follow-up commonly every 1-3 months until stabilized.
  - PDR (non-high-risk or high-risk): urgent referral; treatment (panretinal
    photocoagulation and/or anti-VEGF) typically initiated promptly,
    especially for high-risk features.

## Referral triage summary (useful as an agent decision table)
  - No DR / Mild NPDR without DME -> routine annual screening, no referral
    to specialist required.
  - Moderate NPDR without DME -> referral appropriate but not urgent;
    shortened routine interval.
  - Severe NPDR, any PDR, or DME threatening/involving the fovea ->
    refer to ophthalmologist/retina specialist; treat as time-sensitive.
  - Vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment, rubeosis, or
    neovascular glaucoma -> same-day / emergent ophthalmic referral.

## Modifying factors
  - Rapid, tight glycemic control (including with newer agents such as
    semaglutide) has been associated with an early, transient worsening of
    retinopathy in some patients -- closer monitoring is reasonable after
    starting aggressive glucose-lowering therapy.
  - Puberty is associated with accelerated retinopathy progression and may
    warrant closer follow-up in adolescent patients.
  - Blood pressure and HbA1c control remain the two most important
    modifiable systemic factors for reducing DR onset/progression risk.

## Why referral timing matters clinically
Baseline DR severity is itself the single strongest predictor of who
progresses to sight-threatening disease -- pooled cohort data show roughly
a 2.7x higher 4-year hazard of progression to PDR for moderate vs. mild
NPDR, and roughly 6.5x higher for severe vs. mild NPDR. This is the clinical
rationale behind shortening the follow-up interval as severity increases
rather than using a single fixed annual interval for all patients: the
window in which severe NPDR can silently progress to vision-threatening
PDR is measured in months, not years, in a meaningful fraction of patients.

# Epidemiology and Risk Factors for Diabetic Retinopathy
Source: Synthesized from International Diabetes Federation estimates, WESDR
(Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopathy), UKPDS, ACCORD Eye
Study, and pooled global-prevalence meta-analyses (Yau et al., Diabetes Care
2012; Ting et al., Clin Exp Ophthalmol 2016). Paraphrased summary for
internal knowledge-base use.

## Global burden
Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of vision loss in working-age
adults (roughly ages 20-74) worldwide. Pooled population-based studies
report any-DR prevalence of approximately 30% among people with diabetes,
with proliferative DR (PDR) present in roughly 1% and some degree of
diabetic macular edema in a further 1-7%, though clinic-based (as opposed
to population-based) surveys tend to report notably higher prevalence
since they capture a population already seeking care, sometimes with
symptoms.

## Non-modifiable risk factors
  - **Duration of diabetes**: the single most consistently reported risk
    factor -- longer duration is associated with steadily increasing DR
    prevalence and severity, largely independent of diabetes type.
  - **Age / age at diagnosis**: interacts with duration; younger age at
    type 1 diagnosis is associated with different long-term trajectories
    than later-onset type 2 diabetes.
  - **Genetic predisposition and ethnicity**: prevalence and progression
    rates vary meaningfully across populations (e.g. some Asian and
    Hispanic cohorts show faster progression patterns than others),
    though the specific genetic loci involved remain an active research
    area.
  - **Pregnancy**: independently associated with accelerated retinopathy
    progression, warranting the shortened pregnancy-specific follow-up
    intervals noted in the referral guidance document.
  - **Baseline retinopathy severity itself**: more severe retinopathy at
    any given exam is the strongest single predictor of future progression
    to vision-threatening disease (see icdr_severity_scale.md for
    quantitative progression-risk figures).

## Modifiable risk factors
  - **Chronic hyperglycemia (elevated HbA1c)**: after diabetes duration,
    the most consistently associated modifiable risk factor across
    observational studies and randomized trials; the Diabetes Control and
    Complications Trial (DCCT) attributed a meaningful fraction of DR risk

    any given exam is the strongest single predictor of future progression
    to vision-threatening disease (see icdr_severity_scale.md for
    quantitative progression-risk figures).

## Modifiable risk factors
  - **Chronic hyperglycemia (elevated HbA1c)**: after diabetes duration,
    the most consistently associated modifiable risk factor across
    observational studies and randomized trials; the Diabetes Control and
    Complications Trial (DCCT) attributed a meaningful fraction of DR risk
    to glycemic exposure specifically, though a majority of variance is
    linked to other/interacting factors.
  - **Hypertension**: randomized evidence (e.g. UKPDS, which randomized
    over 1,000 hypertensive type 2 diabetic patients to tight vs.
    conventional blood-pressure targets) demonstrated that tighter blood
    pressure control reduces DR incidence and progression, even though
    observational studies alone have shown a less consistent association.
  - **Dyslipidemia**: elevated total cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL,
    together with reduced HDL, are increasingly recognized as independent
    contributors to DR severity, with some cohorts reporting dyslipidemia
    prevalence as high as 70-97% among people with diabetes.
  - **Nephropathy**: diabetic kidney disease and diabetic retinopathy are
    correlated microvascular complications -- presence of one should raise
    clinical suspicion for the other, and both share duration/hyperglycemia/
    hypertension as common upstream drivers.
  - **Smoking and obesity**: reported as risk factors in some but not all
    cohort studies -- evidence is less consistent than for hyperglycemia,
    hypertension, and dyslipidemia.

## Practical implication for a decision-support system
When patient metadata is available (age, diabetes type/duration, HbA1c,
blood pressure, lipid panel), it should be used to contextualize -- not
override -- the image-derived severity grade. A patient with long diabetes
duration, poor glycemic control, and hypertension who presents with
borderline moderate NPDR findings represents a meaningfully higher

# International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy (ICDR) Disease Severity Scale
Source: Wilkinson et al., "Proposed International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy
and Diabetic Macular Edema Disease Severity Scales," Ophthalmology 2003;
110:1677-1682. (Content below is paraphrased for internal knowledge-base use,
not reproduced verbatim from the original publication.)

## Grading levels

**No apparent retinopathy (Grade 0):** No visible abnormalities on dilated
fundus exam.

**Mild NPDR (Grade 1):** Microaneurysms only. No other lesions present.

**Moderate NPDR (Grade 2):** More than just microaneurysms, but the eye does
not yet meet any of the "severe" criteria below. May include a modest number
of dot/blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, or cotton wool spots.

**Severe NPDR (Grade 3):** Defined by the **4-2-1 rule** -- an eye meeting ANY
ONE of the following three criteria qualifies as severe NPDR, provided there
are no signs of proliferative disease:
  - More than 20 intraretinal hemorrhages in EACH of the four retinal
    quadrants, OR
  - Definite venous beading in TWO OR MORE quadrants, OR
  - Prominent intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) in ONE OR MORE
    quadrants.
An eye meeting two or more of these three criteria simultaneously is
sometimes referred to as "very severe" NPDR and carries an even higher
short-term risk of progression to PDR.

**Proliferative DR / PDR (Grade 4):** One or both of the following:
  - Neovascularization (new vessel growth on the disc, elsewhere in the
    retina, or in the iris/angle), OR
  - Vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage.
PDR is further subclassified as high-risk vs. non-high-risk based on the
location and extent of neovascularization and the presence of vitreous
hemorrhage -- high-risk PDR (e.g. NVD occupying roughly a quarter to a third
of a disc area, or NVD/NVE accompanied by vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage)
warrants urgent treatment.

## Diabetic Macular Edema (DME) is graded separately and can co-occur at any
severity level:
  - **No apparent DME:** No retinal thickening or hard exudates within one
    disc diameter of the fovea.
  - **Mild DME:** Retinal thickening/exudates present but distant from the
    macular center.
  - **Moderate/Severe DME:** Thickening or exudates approaching or involving
    the center of the macula -- this is the threshold most associated with
    risk to central vision and typically triggers anti-VEGF or laser
    consideration regardless of the NPDR/PDR severity grade.

## Clinical progression risk (approximate, pooled from published cohort
studies)
  - Mild NPDR: very low near-term risk of progression to PDR.
  - Moderate NPDR: roughly 20-25% cumulative incidence of PDR over ~4 years;
    faster progression reported in some Southeast Asian cohorts (median
    ~4-5 months to progress moderate -> severe). One large anti-VEGF-naive
    cohort reported 48-month cumulative PDR incidence of ~7.9% for mild
    NPDR, ~20.9% for moderate NPDR, and ~46.8% for severe NPDR at baseline
    -- illustrating a roughly 2.7x hazard increase moderate-vs-mild and a
    ~6.5x hazard increase severe-vs-mild.
  - Severe NPDR: substantially higher short-term risk -- published estimates
    are roughly 15-20% risk of high-risk PDR within 1 year and up to ~40%
    within 3 years.
  - Baseline severity is itself the strongest predictor of progression:
    the Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopathy (WESDR)
    found ~54% less 10-year progression to PDR

## Diabetic Macular Edema (DME): OCT-based staging (modern, supersedes
pure clinical CSME grading in anti-VEGF-era practice)
Source: ETDRS (1985, original CSME definition); ICO Guidelines for
Diabetic Eye Care (2017); DRCR.net / RIDE-RISE trial literature.
Paraphrased summary.

  - **Clinically Significant Macular Edema (CSME)**, the original ETDRS
    definition based on biomicroscopy alone: retinal thickening at or
    within 500 micrometers of the macular center, OR hard exudates at or
    within 500 micrometers of the center if associated with adjacent
    retinal thickening, OR a zone of retinal thickening one disc area or
    larger, any part of which lies within one disc diameter of the
    macular center.
  - **OCT-based grading (current standard)**, per ICO 2017 guidance:
      - No DME: no retinal thickening or hard exudates in the macular
        region.
      - Non-center-involving DME: retinal thickening present but not
        involving the central 1 mm subfield.
      - Center-involving DME: retinal thickening involves the central

    macular center.
  - **OCT-based grading (current standard)**, per ICO 2017 guidance:
      - No DME: no retinal thickening or hard exudates in the macular
        region.
      - Non-center-involving DME: retinal thickening present but not
        involving the central 1 mm subfield.
      - Center-involving DME: retinal thickening involves the central
        1 mm subfield -- this is the threshold most consistently used to
        trigger anti-VEGF therapy in modern practice.
  - **Central Subfield Thickness (CST)** is the quantitative OCT metric
    most commonly used in trials: mean retinal thickness within a 1 mm
    circle centered on the fovea. A CST >= 275 micrometers (time-domain
    OCT convention, e.g. RISE/RIDE trials) or >= 275-320 micrometers
    (spectral-domain OCT, device-dependent) is commonly used as the
    "center-involving" / treatment-eligible threshold, though the exact
    cutoff remains debated and device-dependent -- CST should be
    interpreted relative to the specific OCT platform's normative range
    rather than as a single universal number.
  - DME can occur at ANY DR severity level, including mild NPDR, and its
    course is considered partially independent of the NPDR/PDR severity
    grade -- a system should grade DME status separately rather than
    folding it into the 5-level NPDR/PDR scale.
  - OCT morphological DME patterns (informational, not required for
    triage): sponge-like retinal swelling, cystoid macular edema (most
    common pattern in some cohorts), subretinal fluid, and posterior
    hyaloid traction -- traction patterns may warrant surgical rather than
    injection-based management.

# Retinal Lesion Definitions (for grounding Lesion Analysis Agent outputs)
Source: Standard ophthalmology terminology, consistent with ETDRS and ICDR
literature. Paraphrased for internal knowledge-base use.

## Microaneurysms (MA)
Small, round, focal dilations of retinal capillaries -- typically the
earliest visible sign of diabetic retinopathy. Appear as tiny red dots on
fundus photography.

## Dot and Blot Hemorrhages (HE)
Intraretinal hemorrhages confined to the compact middle retinal layers,
appearing as round ("dot") or larger irregular ("blot") red lesions.
Their quadrant-wise count and distribution is central to the 4-2-1 severe
NPDR rule.

## Hard Exudates (EX)
Yellow-white lipid deposits resulting from leakage of plasma lipoproteins
through damaged capillaries. Clinically important when located within one
disc diameter of the fovea, since this is a defining feature of diabetic
macular edema.

## Cotton Wool Spots (CWS)
Fluffy white patches representing localized nerve fiber layer infarcts from
retinal capillary non-perfusion (microinfarction), rather than a hemorrhage
or lipid deposit. Their presence signals microvascular ischemia.

## Venous Beading (VB)
Focal narrowing and dilation ("sausage-like" segments) of retinal veins,
reflecting significant retinal ischemia. Definite beading in two or more
quadrants is one of the three 4-2-1 criteria for severe NPDR.

## Intraretinal Microvascular Abnormalities (IRMA)
Abnormal, dilated capillary/shunt vessels within the retina that develop in
areas of capillary non-perfusion. Prominent IRMA in one or more quadrants is
one of the three 4-2-1 criteria for severe NPDR, and IRMA is considered a
precursor lesion to frank neovascularization.

## Neovascularization (NV)
New, fragile vessel growth arising from retinal or optic disc vasculature in
response to ischemia-driven VEGF signaling. Defines proliferative diabetic
retinopathy (PDR). Subclassified as NVD (on/near the optic disc) or NVE
(elsewhere in the retina); NVD is associated with higher risk of vision-
threatening complications.

## Neovascularization (NV)
New, fragile vessel growth arising from retinal or optic disc vasculature in
response to ischemia-driven VEGF signaling. Defines proliferative diabetic
retinopathy (PDR). Subclassified as NVD (on/near the optic disc) or NVE
(elsewhere in the retina); NVD is associated with higher risk of vision-
threatening complications.

## Vessel Tortuosity (VT)
Abnormal winding/curvature of retinal vessels, often used as a secondary
severity indicator and studied as an early biomarker of microvascular
stress, though it is not one of the formal ICDR grading criteria.

## Distinguishing IRMA from early neovascularization
This distinction is clinically important and a common source of grading
disagreement between human graders (and a useful check for an automated
system): IRMA vessels are located WITHIN the retina and do not cross the
internal limiting membrane, do not leak significantly on fluorescein
angiography, and do not extend into the vitreous. True neovascularization
grows ON the retinal surface or disc, breaches the internal limiting
membrane, leaks profusely on angiography, and can extend into the
vitreous cavity -- which is why NV (not IRMA) defines the transition from
severe NPDR to PDR. An automated system should treat IRMA as a severe-NPDR
marker and reserve the PDR call specifically for confirmed NV.

## Center-involving vs. non-center-involving hard exudates
Hard exudates are graded differently depending on distance from the
fovea: exudates far from the macula mainly inform NPDR severity staging,
while exudates within one disc diameter of the foveal center are a
defining feature of diabetic macular edema (DME) and should be flagged
separately from the NPDR/PDR severity grade, since DME can co-occur with
any severity level and drives its own referral/treatment pathway (see
aao_followup_referral.md and treatment_protocols.md).

# Treatment Protocols for Diabetic Retinopathy and Diabetic Macular Edema
Source: Synthesized from AAO PPP treatment guidance and DRCR.net (Diabetic
Retinopathy Clinical Research Network) trial literature. Paraphrased summary
for internal knowledge-base use only.

## Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP)
  - Primary treatment for high-risk PDR and often considered for severe
    NPDR / non-high-risk PDR in patients with poor follow-up reliability.
  - Works by ablating peripheral ischemic retina, reducing the angiogenic
    (VEGF) drive behind neovascularization.
  - Can cause peripheral visual field constriction and may transiently
    worsen macular edema -- clinicians should evaluate/treat coexisting DME
    before or alongside PRP when feasible.

## Anti-VEGF Therapy (e.g. ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab)
  - First-line for center-involving diabetic macular edema.
  - Also increasingly used as an alternative or adjunct to PRP for PDR,
    particularly when foveal-threatening DME coexists.
  - Requires repeated intravitreal injections (monthly initially, then
    treat-and-extend or PRN regimens); durability and injection burden are
    key patient-communication points.
  - DRCR.net trials (e.g. Protocol S) found anti-VEGF monotherapy for PDR
    can achieve visual outcomes comparable to PRP, with less peripheral
    field loss, but requires reliable follow-up -- an important referral/
    treatment-planning consideration for patients with limited access to
    care.
  - The RISE and RIDE trials (ranibizumab for DME with CST >= 275
    micrometers on time-domain OCT and corresponding vision loss) showed
    improvement in macular edema within about a week of the first
    injection, with a meaningful proportion of patients gaining >= 15
    ETDRS letters (3 lines) of visual acuity with sustained monthly
    dosing; rescue focal laser was permitted from month 3 onward in
    non-responders.
  - As of the early-to-mid 2020s, an estimated ~90% of US retina
    specialists reported using anti-VEGF as their primary treatment
    for DME-related vision loss, reflecting a broader shift away from

## Focal/Grid Laser
  - Historically used for non-center-involving DME; now often reserved as
    an adjunct or for patients who cannot tolerate ongoing injections.
  - The original ETDRS protocol recommended re-examining DME patients
    every 4-6 months and treating with focal argon laser once CSME
    criteria were met -- this remained standard of care until anti-VEGF
    agents became widely available in the early-to-mid 2010s and is still
    relevant for non-center-involving disease or resource-limited
    settings without ready anti-VEGF access.

## Corticosteroids (intravitreal implants)
  - Considered for DME refractory to anti-VEGF or in pseudophakic patients;
    carries elevated risk of cataract progression and intraocular pressure
    rise, requiring IOP monitoring.

## Vitrectomy
  - Indicated for non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal
    detachment involving or threatening the macula, or combined
    tractional-rhegmatogenous detachment.

## Treatment selection considerations for a decision-support agent
  - Severity grade alone is insufficient -- DME status, prior treatment
    history, patient adherence/follow-up reliability, and systemic factors
    (glycemic control, blood pressure, pregnancy, renal status) all modify
    the appropriate treatment pathway.
  - Any automated system should present treatment options as
    recommendations for physician review, not as autonomous prescribing
    decisions -- final treatment selection is a clinical judgment call by
    a licensed ophthalmologist.
